mainTopic: Stories of the חורבן and ביתר, and the start of the רב–שמואל מחלוקת about buying land from a סיקריקון
overview: This amud continues the גמרא's account of the חורבן and the slaughter at ביתר. It starts with the huge amounts of תפילין boxes found on the dead, explaining that two different counts refer to head-תפילין and arm-תפילין. It then describes children's brains found on one stone and links this to a פסוק in תהלים. The גמרא explains that 'מסולאים בפז' in איכה means the children of ציון were so beautiful they put gold to shame, and tells how Roman noblemen took Jewish children for their beauty. Next come stories of the schoolchildren of ביתר, the young רבי ישמעאל בן אלישע ransomed from a Roman prison, his captive son and daughter who died of grief, and צפנת בת פניאל, whose humiliation leads to the teaching that ה׳ shares His people's pain. Then רב tells of a carpenter's apprentice who tricked his master into divorcing his wife, an injustice that sealed the decree against the Jewish people. Finally the גמרא returns to the משנה about buying land from a סיקריקון, where רב and שמואל disagree about whether a שטר alone makes the purchase valid or a written guarantee (אחריות) is also needed.

steps.title: Baskets of תפילין found on the dead of ביתר
steps.stepSummary: The end of a statement about the תפילין found on the heads of the dead at ביתר, followed by רבי ינאי ברבי ישמעאל's count of three baskets of forty סאה each.
steps.simpleTranslation: [An amount] of תפילין boxes were found on the heads of those killed in ביתר. רבי ינאי ברבי ישמעאל says: three baskets of forty סאה each.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes a sentence from the previous page about the תפילין boxes found on the slain of ביתר. Then רבי ינאי ברבי ישמעאל gives his own count: three baskets, each holding forty סאה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The point is to show how many Jews were killed at ביתר, and that they were Jews who wore תפילין. רבי ינאי ברבי ישמעאל gives a specific measurement, and the next step will bring a ברייתא with different numbers.

keyTerms.meaning: The city where the Romans crushed the בר כוכבא revolt

phrases.english: [An amount] of tefillin boxes were found
phrases.notes: This sentence starts on the previous page, which gave the amount found.

phrases.english: on the heads of those killed in Beitar.
Rabbi Yannai, son of Rabbi Yishmael, says:
Three large baskets
of forty se'ah each.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יַנַּאי בְּרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל אָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the description of ביתר from the previous page
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Three baskets of forty סאה each of תפילין boxes were found on the slain of ביתר.

steps.title: A ברייתא gives a different count
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says there were forty baskets of three סאה each, which seems to clash with רבי ינאי.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught in a ברייתא: forty baskets of three סאה each.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא with different numbers: forty baskets, each of three סאה. This sets up the next step, where the גמרא will show the two reports do not really argue.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי ינאי said three baskets of forty, and the ברייתא says forty baskets of three. The two descriptions do not match, so the reader expects the גמרא to explain how both can be true.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught in a ברייתא (a teaching from the time of the משנה that is outside the משנה)

phrases.english: It was taught in a baraisa:
Forty large baskets
of three se'ah each.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּמַתְנִיתָא תָּנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a second source whose numbers seem to contradict step 1
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Forty baskets of three סאה each were found.

steps.title: Head-תפילין versus arm-תפילין
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says the two reports do not argue: one counts head-תפילין and the other counts arm-תפילין.
steps.simpleTranslation: They do not disagree: this one is talking about head-תפילין, and that one is talking about arm-תפילין.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא settles the clash between steps 1 and 2. Each report is counting a different kind of תפילין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Neither number is wrong. One source describes the head-תפילין that were found and the other describes the arm-תפילין, so both reports can be true together.
steps.whatToRemember: The two counts of תפילין boxes from ביתר are not a disagreement. One counts head-תפילין and the other counts arm-תפילין.

phrases.english: And they do not disagree:
This one is about tefillin of the head,
and that one is about tefillin of the arm.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלָא פְּלִיגִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the apparent contradiction between steps 1 and 2
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (each source refers to a different item)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two counts seem to be two opposing reports of the same thing.
steps.terutzMaskana: One count is head-תפילין and the other is arm-תפילין, so both are correct.

steps.title: Brains found on one stone
steps.stepSummary: רבי אסי says four קבין of brains were found on one stone, and עולא says nine קבין.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אסי said: four קבין of brains were found on one stone. עולא says: nine קבין.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another terrible detail of the slaughter. רבי אסי and עולא give two different amounts of brains found on a single stone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This shows how brutally people were killed: skulls were smashed on one stone. The two אמוראים only differ in the amount, four קבין against nine.

keyTerms.meaning: קב measures (a smaller measure of volume)

phrases.english: Rabbi Asi said:
Four kav of brains
were found on one stone.
Ulla says: nine kav.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אַסִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a new detail about the slaughter
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A great amount of brains (four or nine קבין) was found on one stone.

steps.title: The verse about little ones dashed on the rock
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא (or שילא בר מרי) brings the פסוק in תהלים about Babylon's little ones dashed against the rock as the source.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא said, and some say it was שילא בר מרי: What is the פסוק? 'O daughter of Babylon, marked for devastation, happy is he who repays you... happy is he who seizes and dashes your little ones against the rock.'
steps.whatsHappening: An אמורא brings a פסוק that hints at the brains found on the stone in step 4. The פסוק speaks of little ones dashed against a rock.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'אל הסלע', against the rock, match the image of brains found on one stone. This ties the report of רבי אסי and עולא to a פסוק.

phrases.english: Rav Kahana said,
and some say it was Sheila bar Mari:
What is the verse?
"O daughter of Babylon, marked for devastation,
phrases.notes: תהלים 137:8–9

phrases.english: happy is he who shall repay you, etc.,
happy is he who shall seize and dash
your little ones against the rock."

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי קְרָאָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a פסוק as the source for step 4
steps.raayaObject: The brains found smashed on one stone

steps.title: What does 'comparable to fine gold' mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes 'בני ציון היקרים המסולאים בפז' from איכה and asks what 'מסולאים בפז' means.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'The precious sons of Zion, comparable to fine gold.' What does 'comparable to fine gold' mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new topic with a פסוק from איכה. It asks what the phrase 'מסולאים בפז' means, and the next steps will try to answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase is unclear. It could mean they were literally wrapped in gold, or it could be a picture of how precious they were. The גמרא now explores both readings.

keyTerms.meaning: Compared to, or valued like, fine gold

phrases.english: "The precious sons of Zion,
phrases.notes: איכה 4:2

phrases.english: comparable to fine gold" –
What does "comparable to fine gold" mean?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי מְסוּלָּאִים בַּפָּז
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new discussion of a פסוק in איכה
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The meaning of the phrase 'מסולאים בפז'

steps.title: There is not enough gold in the world
steps.stepSummary: A suggested reading is that they were covered in gold. The גמרא rejects it with the teaching of דבי רבי שילא that only two weights of fine gold came into the world.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say they were covered in fine gold, but the school of רבי שילא said: two איסתירא weights of fine gold came down into the world, one in Rome and one in the whole rest of the world!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries the literal reading, that the people wore gold, and then attacks it. There was far too little fine gold in the world to cover the people of ירושלים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to דבי רבי שילא, the world received only two small weights of fine gold, and half of that went to Rome. So the people of ירושלים could not literally have been covered in פז.

keyTerms.meaning: If you will say (introduces a suggested answer that will be rejected)
Weights of an איסתירא (a small coin weight)

phrases.english: If you say that they were covered in fine gold,
but didn't the school of Rabbi Sheila say:
Two istira-weights of fine gold
came down into the world –
one in Rome,
and one in all the rest of the world!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִילֵּימָא דַּהֲווֹ מְחַפִּי בְּפִיזָּא וְהָאָמְרִי דְּבֵי רַבִּי שֵׁילָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Proposes a literal answer to step 6 and challenges it
steps.kashyaTarget: The literal reading that the people were covered in fine gold
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Only two small weights of fine gold exist in the world, half of them in Rome, so the people of ירושלים could not have been covered in it.

steps.title: Their beauty put gold to shame
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes that 'מסולאים בפז' means the people of ציון were so beautiful that they made fine gold look shameful.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, they would put fine gold to shame with their beauty.
steps.whatsHappening: After rejecting the literal reading, the גמרא gives the real meaning. The people were more beautiful than gold.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק is not describing what they wore. It compares them to gold and says gold loses the comparison, because their beauty made it look poor.

keyTerms.meaning: Put to shame, made look bad

steps.whatToRemember: 'מסולאים בפז' does not mean the people of ציון wore gold, since there was not enough gold in the world. It means their beauty outshone gold.

phrases.english: Rather, they would put fine gold to shame
with their beauty.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא שֶׁהָיוּ מְגַנִּין אֶת הַפָּז בְּיוֹפְיָין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected literal reading with the accepted meaning
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting the פסוק (from a literal description to a comparison)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'מסולאים בפז' means they were literally covered in gold.
steps.terutzMaskana: It means their beauty was so great that it put gold to shame.

steps.title: Roman noblemen and the beautiful Jewish children
steps.stepSummary: Roman noblemen used to look at a beautiful image on a seal during relations. After the destruction, they tied captured Jewish children to their beds instead, because those children were so beautiful.
steps.simpleTranslation: At first, Roman noblemen would hold an image on a seal ring and have relations in their beds while looking at it. From then on, they would bring Jewish children, tie them to the legs of their beds, and have relations.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a sad story that shows just how beautiful the children of ציון were.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 8 said the people of ציון were so beautiful they made fine gold look shameful. This story backs that up: the Romans replaced a carefully made beautiful image with real Jewish children. The point is that these children were seen as more beautiful than any picture.

phrases.english: Originally, the noblemen of Rome
would hold an image engraved on a seal
phrases.notes: They looked at a beautiful picture during relations, hoping to have children who looked like it.

phrases.english: and have relations in their beds;
from then on,
they would bring Jewish children
and tie them to the legs of their beds,
and have relations.

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵעִיקָּרָא, חֲשִׁיבִי דְרוֹמָאֵי הֲווֹ נָקְטִי בִּלְיוֹנָא דְגוּשְׁפַּנְקָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Illustrates the conclusion of step 8 that the people of ציון were more beautiful than fine gold.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that the children of ציון were extraordinarily beautiful.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The story of the Roman noblemen replacing a beautiful image with Jewish children.

steps.title: One captive child asks where this suffering is written
steps.stepSummary: One of the captured children asks his friend where in the Torah this kind of suffering is mentioned.
steps.simpleTranslation: One said to his friend: This, where is it written?
steps.whatsHappening: Two of the captured children talk, and one asks where their suffering appears in the Torah. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even in captivity, the children think in terms of Torah. The question assumes that their suffering must be hinted at somewhere in the תורה.

phrases.english: One said to his friend:
phrases.notes: This is one of the children tied to the beds in the last step.

phrases.english: This, where is it written?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ חַד לְחַבְרֵיהּ: הָא, הֵיכָא כְּתִיבָא?
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story of the captive children from step 9.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Where in the Torah this particular suffering is mentioned.

steps.title: The friend answers with a פסוק from the curses
steps.stepSummary: The friend answers with the פסוק that speaks of every sickness and plague not written in the Torah.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: "Also every sickness and every plague which is not written in the book of this Torah."
steps.whatsHappening: The second child answers by quoting a פסוק from the curses in דברים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק talks about troubles that are not spelled out in the Torah. The child uses it to say that even a suffering not described in detail, like theirs, is included in this general warning.

phrases.english: He said to him:
"Also every sickness and every plague

phrases.aramaic: אֲשֶׁר לֹא כָתוּב בְּסֵפֶר הַתּוֹרָה הַזֹּאת״.
phrases.english: which is not written in the book of this Torah."
phrases.notes: דברים 28:61

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: גַּם כׇּל חֳלִי וְכׇל מַכָּה אֲשֶׁר לֹא כָתוּב בְּסֵפֶר הַתּוֹרָה הַזֹּאת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question asked in step 10.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The suffering is included in the פסוק about every sickness and plague not written in the Torah (דברים 28:61).

steps.title: How far the first child was from that פסוק
steps.stepSummary: The first child asks how far he was from that place in his learning. His friend says a column and a half, and he answers that if he had reached it, he would have known by himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: How far am I from such-and-such a place? He said to him: Go on a column and a half. He said to him: If I had reached it, I would not have needed you.
steps.whatsHappening: The two children finish their conversation, showing how young they were and how far along they were in learning חומש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first child had not yet learned that far in דברים, only a column and a half short. His last line shows that he believed he would have understood the פסוק on his own, which adds to the sadness of children cut off in the middle of learning.

keyTerms.meaning: a column of writing in a scroll

steps.whatToRemember: The captive children were so tied to Torah that even in suffering they discussed where it was written and how far they had learned.

phrases.english: He said: How far am I
from such-and-such a place?
phrases.notes: He means: how far is that פסוק from where I got up to in my learning?

phrases.english: He said to him: Go on a column and a half.
He said to him:
If I had reached it,
I would not have needed you.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר: כַּמָּה מְרַחַיקְנָא מִדּוּכְתָּא פְּלָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the conversation between the two children that began in step 10.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The first child was a column and a half short of the פסוק and would have understood it alone had he reached it.

steps.title: What does the פסוק about the daughters of my city mean?
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה, quoting שמואל in the name of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, asks for the meaning of the פסוק in איכה: my eye affects my soul because of all the daughters of my city.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said that שמואל said in the name of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל: What is meant by what is written: "My eye affects my soul because of all the daughters of my city"?
steps.whatsHappening: A new teaching starts: the גמרא asks what a פסוק in איכה is talking about. This sets up the description of ביתר in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is an opening, not an attack. It points to a פסוק of crying over a city, and the answer will connect it to a specific tragedy.

keyTerms.meaning: what is meant by what is written?

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Shmuel said
in the name of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel:
What is meant by what is written:
"My eye affects my soul
because of all the daughters of my city"?
phrases.notes: איכה 3:51

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל מִשּׁוּם רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל, מַאי דִּכְתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new teaching about the destruction, moving from the captive children to the children of ביתר.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the פסוק in איכה about the daughters of my city refers to.

steps.title: The schoolchildren of ביתר and their terrible end
steps.stepSummary: ביתר had 400 synagogues, each with 400 teachers, each with 400 students. When the enemy came, the children fought back with their pens, and when the enemy won, they wrapped the children in their scrolls and burned them.
steps.simpleTranslation: There were 400 synagogues in the city of ביתר. In each one there were 400 teachers of children, and each teacher had 400 schoolchildren. When the enemy entered there, the children would stab them with their pens. When the enemy won and caught them, they wrapped them in their scrolls and set them on fire.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by describing the huge number of Torah students in ביתר and how they were killed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The numbers show how full of Torah learning ביתר was. The children fought with the only tools they had, their pens. Their death, wrapped in their own scrolls, is the kind of loss that makes the eye cry, as the פסוק says.
steps.whatToRemember: ביתר was full of young Torah learners, and their destruction, burned in their own scrolls, is what the פסוק in איכה mourns.

phrases.english: Four hundred synagogues
were in the city of Beitar,
and in each and every one there were
four hundred teachers of children,
and each and every one had before him

phrases.aramaic: אַרְבַּע מֵאוֹת תִּינוֹקוֹת שֶׁל בֵּית רַבָּן,
phrases.english: four hundred schoolchildren,
and when the enemy entered there
they would stab them with their pens.
phrases.notes: The children are the ones stabbing here, fighting the enemy with their writing pens.

phrases.english: And when the enemy prevailed and caught them,
they wrapped them in their scrolls
and set them on fire.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַרְבַּע מֵאוֹת בָּתֵּי כְנֵסִיּוֹת הָיוּ בִּכְרַךְ בֵּיתֵּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 13 by describing the schoolchildren of ביתר.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק refers to the many schoolchildren of ביתר who resisted with their pens and were wrapped in their scrolls and burned.

steps.title: רבי יהושע בן חנניה hears about a special child in a Roman prison
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא opens a new story. רבי יהושע בן חנניה comes to Rome and is told about a beautiful child being held in prison.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: רבי יהושע בן חנניה once went to the great city of Rome. People told him there was a child in prison with beautiful eyes, a fine appearance, and neatly curled hair.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new story from a ברייתא. This step only sets the scene for what רבי יהושע will do next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The child's beauty is described in detail so we picture an unusual child. Nothing has happened yet. The test of his wisdom comes in the next steps.

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
There was an incident with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya
who went to the great city of Rome.

phrases.aramaic: אָמְרוּ לוֹ: תִּינוֹק אֶחָד יֵשׁ בְּבֵית הָאֲסוּרִים,
phrases.english: They said to him: There is a child in prison
with beautiful eyes and good looks,
and his locks of hair are arranged in curls.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: מַעֲשֶׂה בְּרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן חֲנַנְיָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new captivity story after the story of ביתר's children
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sets the scene: a beautiful Jewish child is being held in a Roman prison.

steps.title: רבי יהושע tests the child with the first half of a פסוק
steps.stepSummary: Standing at the prison door, רבי יהושע quotes a question from ישעיהו: who handed יעקב and ישראל over to plunderers?
steps.simpleTranslation: He went and stood at the prison entrance and said: "Who gave יעקב over to be plundered, and ישראל to robbers?"
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע says the opening of a פסוק out loud, which works as a question. It sets up the child's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק itself is a question, and its answer comes right after it in ישעיהו. Saying it at the prison door checks whether the child knows the continuation.

phrases.aramaic: הָלַךְ וְעָמַד עַל פֶּתַח בֵּית הָאֲסוּרִים,
phrases.english: He went and stood at the entrance of the prison.
He said: "Who gave Jacob over to be plundered
and Israel to robbers?"
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 42:24

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר: מִי נָתַן לִמְשִׁיסָּה יַעֲקֹב וְיִשְׂרָאֵל לְבוֹזְזִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: רבי יהושע acts on what he was told about the child
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the child knows the answer the פסוק gives: who handed ישראל over to its enemies.

steps.title: The child answers with the rest of the פסוק
steps.stepSummary: From inside the prison, the child finishes the פסוק: it was ה׳, because we sinned and did not follow His Torah.
steps.simpleTranslation: The child answered: "Was it not ה׳, the One we sinned against, whose ways they would not walk in, and whose Torah they would not obey?"
steps.whatsHappening: The child answers רבי יהושע by quoting the continuation of the same פסוק. This shows he knows ישעיהו by heart.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The child does more than recite. He explains his own suffering: the exile came from ה׳ because of the people's sins. This shows both knowledge and understanding.

phrases.english: That child answered and said:
"Was it not ה׳, the One we sinned against,
in whose ways they would not walk,
and whose Torah they did not obey?"

steps.triggerLanguage: עָנָה אוֹתוֹ תִּינוֹק וְאָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question posed by the first half of the פסוק
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: ה׳ gave ישראל over to its enemies because they sinned and did not keep His Torah.

steps.title: רבי יהושע swears to ransom the child at any price
steps.stepSummary: Impressed, רבי יהושע predicts the child will become a halachic authority and swears not to leave until he ransoms him.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: I am sure this child will give halachic rulings in ישראל. I swear by the Temple service that I will not move from here until I ransom him, whatever price they set.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע reacts to the child's answer. He makes a prediction and takes an oath.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The quick, fitting answer convinces רבי יהושע that the child is destined for greatness. So he commits to pay any price for him. This shows how much value he placed on a future Torah scholar.

phrases.english: He said: I am certain about him
that he will give halachic rulings in Israel.
By the Temple service!
I will not move from here
until I ransom him
for whatever amount of money they set for him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר: מוּבְטְחַנִי בּוֹ שֶׁמּוֹרֶה הוֹרָאָה בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: רבי יהושע's reaction to the child's wise answer
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יהושע predicts the child will be a halachic authority and swears to ransom him at any cost.

steps.title: The child is ransomed and turns out to be רבי ישמעאל בן אלישע
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע pays a great sum to free the child. Very soon the child is giving rulings, and the ברייתא reveals he was רבי ישמעאל בן אלישע.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said: he did not leave until he ransomed him for a lot of money. Within a few days the child was giving halachic rulings in ישראל. Who was he? רבי ישמעאל בן אלישע.
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends. רבי יהושע keeps his oath, his prediction comes true, and the child's name is revealed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both parts of רבי יהושע's statement come true. The oath is kept because he pays a large ransom. The prediction is fulfilled because the child soon becomes a halachic authority. The final question 'who was he?' reveals the child as the famous רבי ישמעאל בן אלישע.
steps.whatToRemember: The boy in the Roman prison grew up to be רבי ישמעאל בן אלישע. רבי יהושע בן חנניה ransomed him for a large sum because he saw his greatness.

phrases.english: They said: He did not move from there
until he ransomed him for a great deal of money.
And not even a few days passed
before he was giving halachic rulings in Israel.
And who was he? Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרוּ: לֹא זָז מִשָּׁם עַד שֶׁפְּדָאוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows that the oath and the prediction were both fulfilled
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The ransomed child became רבי ישמעאל בן אלישע, a great halachic authority.

steps.title: רבי ישמעאל's son and daughter are captured by two masters
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה, quoting רב, starts a new story. The son and daughter of רבי ישמעאל בן אלישע were taken captive by two different masters, and each master boasts about his slave's beauty.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: The son and daughter of רבי ישמעאל בן אלישע were captured and went to two different masters. Later the two masters met. One said: I have a male slave more beautiful than anyone in the world. The other said: I have a female slave more beautiful than anyone in the world.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a second story about the same family. This step sets up the masters' plan in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first story ended with רבי ישמעאל being freed. Now his own children suffer captivity. The masters' boasting about beauty prepares for their plan to pair the two slaves.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
There was an incident with the son and the daughter
of Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha,
who were taken captive by two different masters.
After some time, the two masters met in one place.
This one said: I have a male slave
whose beauty has no match in the whole world.
And that one said: I have a female slave
whose beauty has no match in the entire world.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב: מַעֲשֶׂה בִּבְנוֹ וּבְבִתּוֹ שֶׁל רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בֶּן אֱלִישָׁע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues with the next generation of רבי ישמעאל's family
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי ישמעאל's son and daughter were enslaved to two masters, and each master boasted about his slave's beauty.

steps.title: The masters try to pair them, and both refuse and weep
steps.stepSummary: The masters plan to marry the two slaves and split the children. Locked in a room, each sits in a corner, refuses because of their כהונה lineage, and they cry all night.
steps.simpleTranslation: The masters said: Let's marry them to each other and divide the children. They put them in a room. He sat in one corner and she sat in another. He said: I am a כהן from a family of כהנים גדולים, shall I marry a slave woman? She said: I am a כהנת from a family of כהנים גדולים, shall I marry a slave? And they cried all night.
steps.whatsHappening: The masters carry out their plan. Each captive separately refuses out of pride in their holy family line. The story continues past this point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both captives react the same way: each sees the other only as a slave and refuses to lower their family's כהונה. Their crying all night shows how painful captivity is, even for children of great people.

keyTerms.meaning: And we will split the children

steps.confusionAlert: Each one thinks the other is just a slave. The story is not finished yet: the next step tells what happens at dawn.

phrases.english: They said: Come, let us marry them to each other
and split the children between us.
They put them into a room.
He sat in this corner,
and she sat in that corner.

phrases.aramaic: זֶה אוֹמֵר: אֲנִי, כֹּהֵן בֶּן כֹּהֲנִים גְּדוֹלִים,
phrases.english: He said: I am a priest, descended from High Priests.
Shall I marry a slave woman?!

phrases.aramaic: וְזֹאת אוֹמֶרֶת: אֲנִי, כֹּהֶנֶת בַּת כֹּהֲנִים גְּדוֹלִים,
phrases.english: And she said: I am a priest's daughter, descended from High Priests.
Shall I be married to a slave?!
And they cried all night.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרוּ: בּוֹא וְנַשִּׂיאֵם זֶה לָזֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The masters act on their boasting by trying to pair the two slaves
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Each captive refused the pairing because of their כהונה lineage, and both wept through the night.

steps.title: At dawn the brother and sister recognize each other and die from grief
steps.stepSummary: When morning comes, the two captives see that they are brother and sister. They fall on each other weeping until they die, and the גמרא applies ירמיה's lament to them.
steps.simpleTranslation: When dawn came, they recognized each other. They fell on each other and cried until their souls left them. About them ירמיה lamented: 'For these I weep; my eye, my eye runs down with water.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the story of רבי ישמעאל בן אלישע's son and daughter. It ends in tragedy, and it ends with a פסוק from איכה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: All night they cried in the dark without knowing who the other was. Morning light shows they are brother and sister, and the shock and pain kill them. The פסוק 'על אלה אני בוכיה' presents their story as one of the things ירמיה was crying over.

keyTerms.meaning: Dawn, the first light of morning

steps.whatToRemember: The story of רבי ישמעאל בן אלישע's children ends with both of them dying from grief. The גמרא uses ירמיה's words in איכה to mourn them.

phrases.english: When dawn broke,
they recognized each other,
and they fell upon each other
and burst out weeping
until their souls left them.
And about them Jeremiah lamented:
"For these I weep,
phrases.notes: איכה 1:16

phrases.english: my eye, my eye runs down with water."

steps.triggerLanguage: כֵּיוָן שֶׁעָלָה עַמּוּד הַשַּׁחַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the story begun in steps 20-21, where the two captives cried all night in separate corners.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The brother and sister die of grief, and ירמיה's lament 'על אלה אני בוכיה' is applied to them.

steps.title: A new story: the woman named צפנת בת פניאל
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש begins a new story about a woman named צפנת בת פניאל and explains what her name means.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש said: There was a story about a woman named צפנת בת פניאל. She was called 'צפנת' because everyone gazed at her beauty. She was called 'בת פניאל' because she was the daughter of a כהן גדול who served in the innermost part of the בית המקדש.
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש opens a new story about a captive woman from a כהונה family. This step only introduces her and explains her name; the story itself comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each part of her name is read as a hint. 'צפנת' sounds like 'צופין' (gaze), so it points to her beauty. 'פניאל' sounds like 'לפני ולפנים' (the innermost place), so it points to her father, the כהן גדול. This shows how special she was, so her fall in the story will be even more painful.

keyTerms.meaning: The innermost place, the קֹדֶשׁ הַקֳּדָשִׁים

phrases.english: Reish Lakish said:
There was an incident with a certain woman,
and her name was Tzafenat bat Peniel;
"Tzafenat" because everyone would gaze at her beauty,
"bat Peniel" because she was the daughter of a High Priest
who served in the innermost place;
phrases.notes: פניאל sounds like לפני ולפנים, the קודש הקדשים, where only the כהן גדול could enter.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ: מַעֲשֶׂה בְּאִשָּׁה אַחַת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After finishing the story of רבי ישמעאל's children, the גמרא opens another story about a captive from a כהונה family.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ריש לקיש introduces צפנת בת פניאל and reads her name as pointing to her beauty and to her father, the כהן גדול.

steps.title: She is abused and put up for sale, and an ugly buyer demands to see her
steps.stepSummary: Her captor abuses her all night and then dresses her in seven garments to sell her. A very ugly man asks to see her beauty, and the seller mocks him, saying no one in the world is as beautiful as she is.
steps.simpleTranslation: Her captor abused her all night. The next day he dressed her in seven garments and took her out to sell her. A very ugly man came and said: Show me her beauty. The seller said: Empty one! If you want to buy her, buy her. There is no beauty like hers in the whole world.
steps.whatsHappening: The story moves forward. The woman is abused and offered for sale, and a buyer asks to see her uncovered.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The seven garments make the coming humiliation worse, because they will be taken off her one at a time. The buyer is described as very ugly, which sharpens the contrast with this beautiful daughter of a כהן גדול. The seller calls him 'ריקא' and tells him to simply trust her beauty and buy.

keyTerms.meaning: Captor, the one who took her captive

phrases.english: that her captor abused her all night.
The next day he dressed her in seven garments,
and brought her out to sell her.
A certain man came
who was extremely ugly,
He said to him: Show me her beauty.
phrases.notes: The buyer is talking to the seller, the captor.

phrases.english: He said to him: Empty one!
If you want to buy, buy,
for there is no beauty like hers in the entire world.

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁנִּתְעַלֵּל בָּהּ שַׁבַּאי כׇּל הַלַּיְלָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues ריש לקיש's story after introducing צפנת בת פניאל.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The captive daughter of a כהן גדול is abused and put up for sale, and an ugly buyer insists on seeing her beauty.

steps.title: Stripped and humiliated, she cries out for the honor of ה׳'s Name
steps.stepSummary: The buyer still insists. Six garments are removed, she tears the seventh herself and rolls in ashes, and she cries out to ה׳: even if You did not pity us, why not pity Your holy Name?
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: Even so. He took six garments off her. She tore the seventh and rolled in the ashes. She said before ה׳: Master of the World, if You had no pity on us, why do You not have pity on the holiness of Your great Name?
steps.whatsHappening: The humiliation reaches its peak, and she answers with a prayer of protest to ה׳. The story continues after this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: She tears the last garment herself and rolls in ashes, which are signs of deep mourning. Her prayer makes a new argument. Even if the Jewish people deserve punishment, shaming the family of the כהן גדול who served before ה׳ also shames ה׳'s own Name.

keyTerms.meaning: She rolled in ashes (a sign of mourning)

steps.whyThisMatters: Her prayer brings out a theme that runs through these stories: the shame of the Jewish people, especially of the כהונה, is also a shame to ה׳'s Name.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לוֹ: אַף עַל פִּי כֵן.
phrases.english: He said to him: Even so.
He stripped six garments off her,
and the seventh, she tore it
and rolled in the ashes,
She said before Him: Master of the World,
if You had no pity on us,
on the holiness of Your (mighty) [great] Name
phrases.notes: Some versions say 'mighty' (round brackets) and some say 'great' (square brackets); the meaning stays the same.

phrases.english: why do You not have pity?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ: אַף עַל פִּי כֵן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the sale scene: the buyer ignores the seller's insult and insists on seeing her, which leads to her humiliation and prayer.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When she is shamed, צפנת בת פניאל prays that even if ה׳ did not pity the people, He should pity His own holy Name.

steps.title: ירמיה's lament: the spoiler came 'upon us'
steps.stepSummary: The story of צפנת ends with ירמיה's lament. The word 'upon us' shows that ה׳ shares the pain.
steps.simpleTranslation: About her, ירמיה lamented: 'Daughter of my people, wear sackcloth and roll in ashes. Mourn as for an only child, a most bitter lament, for suddenly the spoiler will come upon us.' It does not say 'upon you' but 'upon us.' As it were, the spoiler came upon Me and upon you.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes the story of צפנת by applying a פסוק of mourning from ירמיה to her. It then reads one word in that פסוק closely.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק could have said 'upon you,' meaning the Jewish people. It says 'upon us' instead, so ה׳ includes Himself in the disaster. This answers צפנת's own cry from step 25 that ה׳ should pity His holy Name: His Name is hurt too.

keyTerms.meaning: lamented, mourned with a sad song
sackcloth, rough clothing worn when mourning
'as it were,' a careful way of speaking about ה׳

steps.whatToRemember: The גמרא ends the tragic captivity stories with a comfort: when the Jewish people suffer, ה׳, as it were, suffers with them.
steps.whyThisMatters: It ties the stories of the חורבן to ה׳'s own honor. This matches what צפנת cried out in step 25.

phrases.english: And about her, Jeremiah lamented:
"Daughter of my people, gird yourself with sackcloth
and roll in ashes;
make for yourself mourning as for an only child,
a most bitter lament,
for suddenly the spoiler will come upon us"
phrases.notes: ירמיה 6:26

phrases.english: "Upon you" is not stated,
but rather "upon us";
as it were, the spoiler came upon Me and upon you.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְעָלֶיהָ קוֹנֵן יִרְמְיָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the צפנת story from steps 23 to 25 with a פסוק, the same way step 22 closed the brother-and-sister story.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The פסוק says 'upon us,' which teaches that ה׳ shares in the suffering of His people.

steps.title: A new story: the apprentice who desired his master's wife
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה, quoting רב, asks what a פסוק in מיכה means. He begins a story about a carpenter's apprentice who wanted his master's wife.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: What does the פסוק 'And they oppress a man and his house, and a person and his inheritance' mean? There was a man who set his eyes on his master's wife. He was a carpenter's apprentice.
steps.whatsHappening: A new story starts here. רב uses it to explain a פסוק about oppressing a man and his household.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק talks about stealing a man's 'house,' and חז"ל often use 'house' to mean a wife. So the story will show a man literally taking someone's wife. The setup tells us the main problem: the apprentice wants his own master's wife.

keyTerms.meaning: and they oppressed, cheated, took by force
his inheritance, what belongs to him

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
What is the meaning of what is written:
"And they oppress a man and his house,
phrases.notes: מיכה 2:2

phrases.english: and a person and his inheritance"?
There was an incident with a certain man
who set his eyes on his master's wife,
and he was a carpenter's apprentice.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב, מַאי דִּכְתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new story after the captivity stories are finished.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The פסוק 'they oppress a man and his house' is explained through a story of an apprentice who desired his master's wife.

steps.title: The loan trap and the apprentice's lie
steps.stepSummary: The master needs a loan. The apprentice has the wife sent to him, keeps her three days, and then lies that youths abused her on the way home.
steps.simpleTranslation: Once his master needed to borrow money. The apprentice said: Send your wife to me and I will lend it to her. He sent his wife, and the apprentice stayed with her three days. The apprentice went ahead and came to his master. The master asked: Where is my wife whom I sent to you? He answered: I sent her back right away, but I heard that young men abused her on the way.
steps.whatsHappening: The story continues with the apprentice's plan. He uses the loan as an excuse to get the wife alone, and then he invents a story to cover up.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The apprentice takes advantage of his master's need for money. By arriving before the wife and blaming strangers on the road, he plants the idea that she is now forbidden to her husband. This prepares the next step, where he advises divorce.

phrases.english: One time (his master) needed to borrow,
phrases.notes: Some versions don't have the word in round brackets, but either way it is the master who needs the loan.

phrases.english: he said to him: Send your wife to me
and I will lend to her.
He sent his wife to him,
and he stayed with her for three days.
He went ahead and came to him,
phrases.notes: The apprentice got to the master before the wife returned home.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לוֹ: אִשְׁתִּי שֶׁשִּׁיגַּרְתִּי לְךָ הֵיכָן הִיא?
phrases.english: He said to him: My wife whom I sent to you, where is she?
He said to him: I sent her away right away,
and I heard that the youths abused her on the way.
phrases.notes: תינוקות here means rough young men, not babies.

steps.triggerLanguage: פַּעַם אַחַת הוּצְרַךְ רַבּוֹ לִלְוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story from step 27 and shows how the apprentice carries out his plan.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The apprentice uses a loan to get his master's wife alone, then lies that strangers abused her.

steps.title: The apprentice advises divorce, funds it, and marries her
steps.stepSummary: The apprentice tells the master to divorce his wife and lends him money for her כתובה. Then the apprentice marries her himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: The master said: What should I do? The apprentice said: If you take my advice, divorce her. The master said: Her כתובה is large. He said: I will lend you the money, and you give her the כתובה. The master went and divorced her, and the apprentice went and married her.
steps.whatsHappening: The trap closes. The apprentice talks the master into a divorce, pays for it with a loan, and takes the wife for himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The only thing holding the master back is that the כתובה costs a lot of money. The apprentice removes that problem with a loan. Now the master has lost his wife and also owes money to the man who took her, which is exactly what 'oppressing a man and his house' means.

keyTerms.meaning: her כתובה, the money owed to a wife at divorce

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the master gave the כתובה from his own money. It came from a loan from the apprentice, so the master now owes him money.

phrases.english: He said to him: What should I do?

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לוֹ: אִם אַתָּה שׁוֹמֵעַ לַעֲצָתִי, גָּרְשָׁהּ.
phrases.english: He said to him: If you listen to my advice, divorce her.
He said to him: Her marriage contract is large.
He said to him: I will lend you the money,
and you give her her marriage contract.
This one went and divorced her,
and he went and married her.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ: מָה אֶעֱשֶׂה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the apprentice's scheme that began in step 28, using the lie to get the divorce.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Through lies and a loan, the apprentice gets his master to divorce his wife and then marries her himself.

steps.title: The master is forced to serve drinks at his former wife's table
steps.stepSummary: The master cannot repay the loan. The apprentice makes him work off the debt by serving drinks to the apprentice and the woman, and the master's tears fall into their cups.
steps.simpleTranslation: When the loan came due and the master could not pay it back, the apprentice told him: 'Come work for me to pay off your debt.' The apprentice and the woman would sit, eat and drink, while the master stood and poured their drinks. His tears dropped from his eyes into their cups.
steps.whatsHappening: The story reaches its painful climax. The master loses his wife and his money, and now he must serve the very people who wronged him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every step of the plan has worked against the master. He divorced his wife because of a lie, borrowed her כתובה money from the man who lied, and now pays that debt by serving them. The tears in the cups show his helpless pain, and the next step builds on that.

keyTerms.meaning: Work with me to pay off your debt

phrases.english: When its time came
phrases.notes: He means the time to repay the loan the master took for the כתובה.

phrases.english: and he did not have the means to repay it,
he said to him:
Come and work with me for your debt.
And they would sit
phrases.notes: 'They' are the apprentice and the woman, who is now his wife.

phrases.english: and eat and drink,
while he would stand
and pour drinks for them,
and tears would drop from his eyes
and fall into their cups.

steps.triggerLanguage: כֵּיוָן שֶׁהִגִּיעַ זְמַנּוֹ וְלֹא הָיָה לוֹ לְפוֹרְעוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story from step 29, where the master borrowed money from the apprentice to pay the כתובה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The wronged master is reduced to serving his former wife and her new husband, weeping as he serves.

steps.title: The decree is sealed because of this sin
steps.stepSummary: At that moment the decree against the Jewish people was sealed. Some say the reason was 'two wicks in one lamp.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Because of that moment, the decree was sealed. Some say it was sealed because of 'two wicks in one lamp.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא ends the story by naming the point at which the punishment became final. It then brings a second opinion about which part of the story caused it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first opinion points to the cruelty: the master wept at the table, and nobody stopped the injustice. The second opinion points to the forbidden relationship: the woman was with the apprentice while still married to the master. This explains the פסוק in מיכה that רב began with in step 27.

keyTerms.meaning: A sentence, a decree of punishment
Two wicks in one lamp, a gentle way of describing adultery

steps.whatToRemember: The story of the apprentice ends by naming what sealed the decree of the חורבן: either the cruelty to the weeping master, or the sin of 'two wicks in one lamp.'

phrases.english: And because of that moment
the sentence was sealed.
And some say:
because of two wicks in one lamp.
phrases.notes: A gentle way of saying she was with the apprentice while still married to the master.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְעַל אוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה נִתְחַתֵּם גְּזַר דִּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the meaning of the scene in step 30 and closes the story that began in step 27.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The decree was sealed either at the moment of the master's tears or because of the forbidden relationship ('two wicks in one lamp').

steps.title: רב limits the משנה about buying from a סיקריקון
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the משנה about buying land from a סיקריקון. רב says the purchase is void only when the owner just told the buyer 'go take possession.' A purchase made with a שטר is valid.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: 'If one bought from a סיקריקון, etc.' רב said: The משנה only meant a case where the owner told him, 'Go, take possession and acquire it.' But if he sold it with a document, the buyer acquires it.
steps.whatsHappening: The אגדה is finished, and the גמרא goes back to the halacha in the משנה. רב narrows the משנה's ruling so that it covers only one kind of sale.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, a person bought land from a סיקריקון and then bought it again from the original owner, and the purchase is void. רב says this applies only when the owner just told him to take possession. An owner who said only that can claim he never really meant to sell, but writing a שטר shows he truly sold the land.

keyTerms.meaning: A violent man who took land from its owner by force
They only taught this (in the case of...); a phrase that narrows a ruling
Take possession and acquire, acquiring land by doing an act of ownership on it
A written document, here a bill of sale
He acquires it; the purchase is valid

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think רב disagrees with the משנה. He agrees the purchase can be void, and he only limits it to a sale done without a שטר.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the מחלוקת between רב and שמואל about how strong a sale must be to count when a victim sells land that was already taken by force.

phrases.english: "If one bought from a Sicarius, etc.":
Rav said:
They taught this only
where he said to him:
"Go, take possession and acquire,"
but with a document, he acquires.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָקַח מִן הַסִּיקָרִיקוֹן וְכוּ׳ אָמַר רַב לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the אגדה and returns to the halacha in the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The purchase is void only when the sale was 'go, take possession and acquire.' A sale with a שטר is valid.

steps.title: שמואל requires a written guarantee
steps.stepSummary: שמואל disagrees with רב. Even with a שטר the buyer does not acquire the land unless the owner also writes him a guarantee (אחריות).
steps.simpleTranslation: And שמואל said: Even with a document he still does not acquire it, unless the owner writes him a guarantee.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל gives a stricter view than רב. A plain שטר is not enough to make this sale valid.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רב, a שטר is enough proof that the sale is real. For שמואל, only a guarantee shows the owner truly meant to sell: he promises to pay the buyer back if a creditor takes the field. Taking on that risk shows a real sale and not a sale made under pressure.

keyTerms.meaning: Even... also; a phrase that extends a ruling further
A guarantee that the seller will pay the buyer back if the field is taken by the seller's creditor

steps.whatToRemember: רב: a שטר makes the purchase valid. שמואל: even a שטר is not enough without a written guarantee (אחריות).

phrases.english: And Shmuel said:
even with a document, he also does not acquire,
until he writes him a guarantee.
phrases.notes: A guarantee means the seller promises to pay the buyer back if the seller's creditor takes the field.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּשְׁמוּאֵל אָמַר אַף בִּשְׁטָר נָמֵי לֹא קָנָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with רב in step 32 and sets a stricter requirement.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even a sale with a שטר is void unless the owner writes in a guarantee (אחריות).
